## Objectives {#objectives}

By the end of this session you can:

- Request data from an API and turn the JSON response into a data frame.
- Store an API key in `~/.Renviron` and read it from R.
- Page through results within the rate limit, and compare the rows you
  received with the total the API reports.
- Save each raw response so the pipeline reruns from disk.
- Send a prompt to a large language model through its provider's API
  from R, read the reply, and count the tokens it used.
- Convert UTC timestamps to local time.

## What we cover {#coverage}

- Published work built on an API, a service that lets your program
  request data from another computer and receive a structured reply.
  [Akbar et al. (AER, 2023)](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20181662)
  queried Google Maps for 57 million simulated car trips in 180 Indian
  cities, choosing destinations through the Google Places API, to measure
  travel speed and congestion, then compared them with data on actual
  trips.
  [Fujiwara, Müller & Schwarz (JEEA, 2024)](https://doi.org/10.1093/jeea/jvad058)
  pulled the profiles of about 658,000 followers of a festival's Twitter
  account through Twitter's API, and used their join dates and locations
  to estimate Twitter's effect on US presidential votes. From finance,
  [Lopez-Lira & Tang (JFE, 2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2026.104335)
  sent firm news headlines to a large language model (a program trained
  on vast amounts of text that writes a reply to what you send) through
  its provider's API, scored each as good or bad news, and tested whether
  the scores predict stock returns.
- Every call has the same shape: a key, a request and a response. The
  response carries a status code (200 means it worked, 429 too many
  requests) and, when it worked, data in JSON, a plain-text format of
  named values and nested lists that you turn into a data frame.
- Endpoints (the web address that answers one kind of request) and query
  parameters (named values, such as a year or a state, that narrow what
  comes back). Long results arrive in pages you request one after another
  (pagination), within a rate limit, the most requests a service accepts
  from you per minute, hour or day. Compare the number of rows you
  collected with the total the API reports.
- An API key is a private string that identifies you and counts your
  requests. Keys live in `~/.Renviron` as environment variables (named
  values set outside your code and loaded when R starts) and are read with
  `Sys.getenv()`, so they never appear in a script or a commit.
- Saving the raw response, the reply exactly as the server sent it, with
  `saveRDS()` and reading it back with `readRDS()`, so the pipeline still
  runs when the server changes or goes down.
- A model call sends a prompt (the instructions and material in one
  request) from R to a large language model, with its key stored the same
  way. Read the raw reply to verify anything parsed from it. The same
  request sent twice can come back worded differently, and many current
  models do not let you turn that variation off, so the saved reply is
  the record. Each reply reports its usage in tokens, the chunks of text
  a model reads, writes and bills by.
- Timestamps that arrive in UTC, the world reference clock, converted to
  local time with `lubridate`, daylight saving included.
